operations.name: Mateen Abdul Shaheed

expected.name: Mateen Abdul Shaheed
expected.description:
Mateen Abdul Shaheed is a black youth, born and raised in Portland. On November 10th, 2016, Portland filled with over ten thousand people hitting the streets in protest to the election of Donald Trump; 20-year-old Shaheed was one of them. In the Pearl District, one of Portland’s most gentrified neighborhoods, there were much acts vandalizing car dealerships and city infrastructure in response to the city's history of racism. In the coming days, there would be many protests and confrontations between the people and the police. 

Mateen is accused of causing damage in a car dealership and other infrastructure items such as electrical boxes in the city. He pleaded guilty to five counts of first and second-degree criminal mischief and was sentenced to 18 months in prison. He was released in 2018.
expected.body: Custody-source review October 13, 2026: KTVZ's contemporaneous report of Portland Police's announcement identifies the Tuesday, November 15, 2016 arrest and booking into Multnomah County Jail. The existing arrest and admission dates are retained. The unrelated Edna Mahan Correctional Facility for Women attachment has been cleared. An independently documented sentencing day and actual release date have not been established; sentence-length arithmetic and an unsupported exact release are not substituted for those records.

expected.name: Karl Smith
expected.description: Karl Smith was 27 at the time of the Griffiss action and a member of the Jonah House resistance community in Baltimore. He had previously been imprisoned with James Cunningham for 60 days for trespassing at the Trident plant in Bangor, Washington, before they both joined Jonah House.
expected.body:
Separate Pentagon and Griffiss custody records

The appellate opinion names Smith among the seven Griffiss defendants and dates their action and arrest to November 24, 1983, correcting the previously stored November 23. It specifies his concurrent three-year terms and identifies Judge Howard G. Munson. United States v. Allen, 760 F.2d 447, opening factual account. The original August 2, 1984 Nuclear Resister reports that sentence was imposed July 16. Neither source establishes Smith's initial jail-admission date or exact final discharge day, so those fields are left unknown. Contemporary sentencing report, front page.

The original May 9, 1984 Nuclear Resister separately reports that Smith served 30 days in the D.C. Jail after conviction for blockading Pentagon doors during the preceding December's Holy Innocents actions, was released May 4, and then headed to the Griffiss trial. This is recorded as a distinct case, not the end of Griffiss imprisonment. No admission day is back-calculated. Pentagon release report, printed page 6.

The former 60-day total is removed from the Griffiss record: the existing biography associates that duration with an earlier Bangor trespass case, not this prosecution. The July 18, 1986 Nuclear Resister lists Smith among previously listed prisoners who had been released, but does not give his individual discharge day. That publication date is not entered as his release date. No independently identified photograph has yet been verified. Contemporary released-prisoner roster, printed page 3.

Official federal endpoint identified

Karl Smith's own solidarity letter in The Witness, April1985, indexed primary text identifies01268-052 and Griffiss Plowshares7. That uniquely documented number visibly matched KARL SMITH in the authorized official BOP locator on October12,2026 and supplies July11,1986 as its custody endpoint. The earlier original recently-released newsletter was already visually reviewed. No portrait is provided by the locator; missing identified reusable photograph and other earlier individual episodes remain unresolved.

operations.name: Christian Damian Cerna-Camacho

expected.name: Christian Damian Cerna-Camacho
expected.description:
Christian Damian Cerna-Camacho, a United States citizen from Boyle Heights in Los Angeles, was 28 when federal prosecutors accused him of punching a Customs and Border Protection officer during the June 7, 2025 protest against immigration raids in Paramount, California.

He was not arrested at the protest. Agents came for him four days later, on June 11, 2025, pinning his car between two unmarked vehicles on Whittier Boulevard in Boyle Heights with guns drawn and deploying a chemical device while his wife and their two young children were inside. The Department of Homeland Security then published its own high-resolution video of the operation on social media, calling him a “violent rioter” — footage which in fact showed him surrendering at once. Bail was refused at his first appearance, and he spent about a week in custody before being released to house arrest with GPS monitoring.

He pleaded guilty on December 16, 2025 to assault on a federal officer, a felony carrying up to eight years. At sentencing in 2026 the court rejected that framing. A federal judge described the department’s publicity campaign as a “vindictive effort” and “extrajudicial punishment”, the felony was reduced to a misdemeanor count of simple assault on a federal officer, and he received probation rather than prison.

expected.body:
Trident Nein dates and separate proceedings

Participant Art Laffin dates the action and arrests to July 5, 1982. The contemporary sentencing report dates the original disposition to November 9, 1982. A sentence is not treated as a verified prison-admission date.

Sources: Art Laffin, July 2022 eyewitness retrospective; Revolutionary Worker, November 12, 1982, pages 1–2.

Original archival custody and release evidence

The Nuclear Resister issue 12 names all nine participants and reports seven weeks in jail followed by August 26, 1982 recognizance release. Initial custody is July 5–August 26, not an uninterrupted stay through 1983.

Issue 13 records the November 9 sentence as suspended to time served. Issue 15 documents February 2, 1983 revocation and renewed imprisonment. The intervening recognizance period is excluded from time imprisoned.

Actual later prison release: 1983-05-27. This is not the end of the entire sentence.

Sources: issue 12, October 18, 1982, printed page 4 (PDF page 6); issue 13, November 30, 1982, page 4; issue 14, January 14, 1983, page 3; issue 15, March 9, 1983, printed page 6 (PDF page 8); issue 16, April 17, 1983, printed page 10 (PDF page 11); issue 17, June 6, 1983, page 5.

expected.name: Reuben Taylor
expected.description: Reuben Taylor was a young Black man from Chicago's South Side and a member of De Mau Mau, an organization formed by Black servicemen in Vietnam to resist racism in the U.S. military. He was 22. In 1972 he was among those arrested and prosecuted in a series of murders of white people in the Chicago suburbs (including a family of four in Barrington Hills and a family of three in Monee). The Black Panther (November 1972) reported the case as racist sensationalism — built without clear evidence and tied to State's Attorney Edward Hanrahan's re-election campaign — that had "convicted" the defendants in the press before trial. The prosecutions were heavily contested; several of the De Mau Mau defendants were convicted in 1973.

expected.name: William Coffin
expected.description: William Coffin was one of the 74 Industrial Workers of the World members held in the Snohomish County jail and charged with murder after the Everett Massacre. On November 5, 1916, some 300 Industrial Workers of the World members sailed from Seattle to Everett, Washington aboard the steamers Verona and Calista to support a shingle-weavers' strike and the IWW's free-speech fight. At the Everett dock, Snohomish County sheriff Donald McRae and a posse of armed vigilantes opened fire on the Verona, killing at least five Wobblies and wounding dozens. The returning IWW members were arrested, and 74 were charged with the murder of two deputies (Jefferson Beard and Charles Curtis) killed in the gunfire. Only Thomas H. Tracy was brought to trial; after his acquittal on May 5, 1917, the charges against the others were dropped. At the time of the massacre he was 34, a motorman, born in California.

operations.name: Edward Hoffmans

expected.name: Edward Hoffmans
expected.description: Edward Charles Hoffmans — the surname really does end in s — was 31 at the time of the Chicago 15 action, living in Iowa City, working as a draft counselor after teaching English at the University of Northern Iowa, and already nationally controversial for publicly advocating draft resistance. Before dawn on May 25, 1969 he and fourteen others entered the Selective Service offices at 2355 West 63rd Street in Chicago, removed roughly fifty sacks containing about 40,000 draft records and burned them in the alley, then stayed at the scene singing until police arrested them and took them to Cook County Jail. A federal grand jury indicted all fifteen on June 3, 1969 on four counts: willful damage to federal property, destruction of federal records, interference with the Military Selective Service Act, and conspiracy. His case did not follow the ten defendants convicted by the jury in June 1970: on June 3, 1970 Judge Edwin Robson found him incompetent and severed his case, committing him to the federal medical center at Springfield, Missouri, where he was found competent shortly after arriving and released on bond on August 21 — a commitment of about 79 days. On November 18, 1970 he pleaded guilty under an agreement calling for three years in federal prison with no probation, surrendered on January 8, 1971, and served at the Federal Correctional Institution at Sandstone, Minnesota, where he was confirmed still imprisoned on February 16, 1972; the date of his actual release has not been found. His reported ages place his birth in 1937 or 1938. He later became a prominent Chicago disability-rights activist with ADAPT, and Access Living’s 2019 annual report lists donations in his memory, establishing that he had died by that year; no obituary or exact date of death has been located.

Federal record and admission-date clarification

Arrest, conviction, sentence and prison admission are distinct events. The database's automatic arrest-anchored elapsed-day calculation is not evidence of uninterrupted custody since the arrest.

expected.description:
Dottie Mather was identified in a February 2, 1972 Washington Post interview as a 21-year-old woman who had served 21 months at Alderson Federal Reformatory for Women after a drug-related arrest in Washington, D.C. The article did not identify the specific charge, sentence imposed, or dates of her arrest and admission.

Mather said an initial parole examination resulted in what she called a “20-month contract.” At a second examination in September 1971, she deliberately presented herself as less knowledgeable because she believed that was necessary to secure parole. She said the examination lasted about ten minutes and that parole was granted. The exact date she physically left Alderson remains unknown.

Mather also alleged that prison officials disapproved of her association with prisoners she described as “the political people.” She said she had been promised work as a keypunch operator with the Central Committee for Conscientious Objectors and recalled a parole examiner disparaging that plan. The available clipping documents her account of political association affecting parole treatment; it does not establish that the original drug prosecution was politically motivated or that she later worked for the organization. Her full legal name, birth and death dates, and later life remain unverified.

operations.name: Lorena Barnum Sabbs

expected.name: Lorena Barnum Sabbs
expected.description:
Lorena Barnum Sabbs was one of the Black school-aged girls imprisoned in southwest Georgia in 1963 after participating in demonstrations against racial segregation in Americus. Authorities moved girls arrested during the campaign to the Lee County Stockade in neighboring Leesburg, concealed their location from their families, and held them without formal criminal charges. Her individual custody duration is documented in a contemporary sworn statement or closely contemporaneous record. The children endured overcrowding, inadequate food and water, broken sanitation, little or no bedding, and delayed medical attention. SNCC photographer Danny Lyon documented the confinement through the bars; publication of his photographs helped force public attention and the girls’ release.

Her September 13, 1963 sworn statement says she was 11 and confined in the stockade from August 31 to September 1. She described 32 children sharing two drinking cups, unusable toilets, and rusty-tasting water.

Photo: Servant Emannu'el Branch / BHBP News, September 27, 2019. Original-image crop; identified by the source (first of five survivors in foreground, from left). Source: https://bhbpnews.com/historical-marker-for-stolen-girls-held-at-leesburg-ga-stockade-p518-203.htm . Copyright status unconfirmed; used for educational biographical identification at the site owner's direction. No permission or open license claimed.
expected.body:
## The Leesburg Stockade

In the summer of 1963, young people in Americus, Georgia demonstrated against segregation, including the Martin Theater’s separate entrances and ticket windows. Local authorities arrested hundreds of participants. More than 30 Black girls were held at different times in the Lee County Stockade in nearby Leesburg without formal charges or a court hearing.

Contemporary sworn statements show that the girls did not all enter or leave together. They describe changing populations of roughly 32 to 35 children, overflowing or unusable toilets, contaminated bedding, undercooked food, rusty water, and periods when the children slept directly on concrete. The profile’s custody dates and duration are therefore individual where evidence permits; no universal 45-day range has been imposed.

SNCC photographer Danny Lyon photographed the girls and the stockade conditions. The resulting photographs circulated through movement publications and the Black press and helped expose where the children were being held.

expected.description: Marvin Cheatom Jr. was a 16-year-old Black Panther in Des Moines when he and his mother, welfare-rights organizer Joeanna Cheatom, were arrested during the December 27, 1968 raid on the Panther headquarters. He faced arson charges arising from the Jewett Lumber fire and was held on a $20,000 bond. expected.body:
Jewett Lumber case

The prosecution arose from the October 1968 Jewett Lumber Company fire in Des Moines. Contemporary reporting also associated the investigation with a fire at an A&P grocery store. The Militant characterized the arrests as an attack on Black organizing; that political interpretation is attributed to the newspaper, rather than treated as a court finding.

The December 27 arrest and $20,000 bond were reported in The Militant. The Daily Iowan's January 7 issue also reported that Joeanna and Marvin were still in jail in lieu of bond. The trial with Charles Knox began April 18. On April 21 Judge James P. Denato dismissed the case for insufficient evidence, following the defense's challenge to uncorroborated accomplice testimony. A later police account described directed not-guilty rulings. The dismissal date is a court outcome, not a verified jail-release date.

Available records document this historical case. No verified current detention is recorded. Custody duration and unsupported personal details are left blank.

The Daily Iowan reported Jones's prosecution testimony during the April 18, 1969 trial and that he was being held in Polk County Jail. He admitted involvement in the fire and alleged that Knox and Joeanna Cheatom accompanied him. The judge dismissed their case for insufficient corroborating evidence. In the 1970 House hearing, sergeant Paul Gladson named the remaining defendant as Calvin Johns Jr., reported a guilty plea and a ten-year reformatory sentence. The contemporary newspaper spells the name Calvin Jones Jr.; both source spellings are recorded here. The sentence is not entered as ten years actually served.

Available records document this historical case. No verified current detention is recorded. Custody duration and unsupported personal details are left blank.

Sources

  • The Militant, January 10, 1969, page 3
  • The Daily Iowan, January 7, 1969
  • The Daily Iowan, April 19, 1969, page 1
  • The Daily Iowan, April 22, 1969, page 1
  • 1970 House hearing, printed pages 4844–4845
  • The Annals of Iowa, Winter 2010, page 73

Record spelling: Calvin Jones Jr. in the 1969 newspaper; Calvin Johns Jr. in the 1970 police testimony.

expected.body:
Los Angeles Panther raids and detention

Paul Redd was detained after the Central Avenue raid. The Party newspaper reports that he was confined in New County Jail’s adjustment center after drawing revolutionary art on jail walls. This is the 19-year-old Los Angeles defendant in 1969, not Oakland-born prison organizer Paul Alwyn Redd Jr., born in 1956.

The December 8, 1969 Los Angeles police raids targeted Black Panther premises at Central Avenue, the Toure Community Center and a residence on 55th Street. The Party denounced the operation as political repression. Contemporary Party reports are attributed as such; their allegations of mistreatment are not presented as independent court findings.

Individual verdicts, physical release dates and time actually detained are recorded only where supported. The broader trial included acquittals on serious counts and some weapons-conspiracy convictions. It would be inaccurate to describe every raid defendant as acquitted of every charge.

Sources

  • The Black Panther, December 20, 1969, printed pages 2, 10–11 and 13: named custody reports
  • The Black Panther, December 27, 1969, printed page 15: LA 18 defense roster
